claim: Tax year 2026, married couple filing jointly, two children under 13, at least $7,500 of child care, all income from wages. Option A: put $7,500 through a workplace dependent care assistance account (excluded from wages, saving income tax and 7.65% employee payroll tax; by law it reduces the $6,000 credit-eligible expense cap to zero). Option B: no account; claim the child and dependent care credit on $6,000 of expenses at the new rate schedule (50% reduced to 35% by AGI $45,000; for joint returns falling toward 20% above $150,000). At $100,000 of wages the credit is $2,100 while the account saves $1,474 (12% + 7.65% on $7,500), so the credit leaves the family about $626 better off. But computing the whole federal return (income tax, nonrefundable and refundable child tax credit, earned income credit, employee payroll tax) the credit wins only for wages from about $70,500 to $139,000. Below that band the account wins because the care credit cannot be refunded and the account lowers earned income and AGI, which raises the earned income credit (at $80,000 of wages the credit still wins by $626; at $40,000 the account wins by about $2,153). Above it the account wins because each excluded dollar saves 22% income tax (at $180,000 of wages the account wins by about $604). The $6,000 expense cap has not changed since tax year 2003; carried forward with consumer prices it would be about $10,731. Sources: 26 U.S.C. 21, 129, 24, 32, 3101; Rev. Proc. 2025-32 (IRB 2025-45); IRS IR-2025-103.

numbers.definition: Child and dependent care credit for a joint return with AGI $100,000 and two qualifying children: applicable percentage (50 minus 1 point per $2,000 or fraction of AGI over $15,000, not below 35; then minus 1 point per $4,000 or fraction of AGI over $150,000, not below 20) = 35%, times $6,000.
$7,500 x (0.12 + 0.0765): income tax at the 12% bracket plus employee Social Security (6.2%) and Medicare (1.45%) tax avoided on $7,500 excluded dependent care assistance.

NetCost(FSA) - NetCost(credit) at wages W = $100,000, where NetCost = federal income tax after all credits (can be negative) + 0.0765 x wages counted for payroll tax. FSA path: wages and AGI = W - 7,500, credit expense cap = max(0, 6,000 - 7,500) = 0. Credit path: wages and AGI = W, care credit = min(tax, rate(AGI) x 6,000). Income tax = 2026 joint schedule (10% to 24,800; 12% to 100,800; 22% to 211,400; 24% to 403,550; 32% to 512,450; 35% to 768,700; 37% above) on max(0, AGI - 32,200). Credits in order: care credit (nonrefundable), child tax credit 2 x 2,200 nonrefundable up to remaining tax, refundable remainder = min(unused CTC, 2 x 1,700, 0.15 x max(0, earned - 2,500)); earned income credit (two children, joint) = max(0, min(7,316, (7,316/18,290) x earned) - 0.2106 x max(0, max(AGI, earned) - 31,160)). Positive = credit path costs less.

assumptions: Tax year 2026 rules as in force on 2026-09-29 (U.S. Code) and Rev. Proc. 2025-32.
Married filing jointly; two qualifying children under 13; both spouses work; child care spending of at least $7,500 (e.g., $15,000), so both options are fully used.
All income is wages; no other income, deductions or credits; standard deduction; each spouse below the 2026 Social Security wage base.
The employer plan offers the full $7,500 and the family either uses the full $7,500 account or no account (a mix is never better: the credit cap falls dollar for dollar with the account).
Earned income credit computed with the Rev. Proc. 2025-32 two-child amounts and the statutory 40% / 21.06% rates (the published IRS tables round slightly differently).

Federal only: state income tax is ignored (in states that exclude the account from state wages, the account gains extra, e.g. about $375 at a 5% state rate, which would narrow but not close the $626 gap).
Payroll tax saved by the account also slightly lowers future Social Security benefit credits; not valued here.
